title: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — An Apartment in the Duke's Palace
openingText: If music be the food of love, play on. Give me an excess of it, so that, glutted, my appetite may sicken and die.
about:
Twin siblings Viola and Sebastian are separated in a shipwreck on the coast of Illyria. Each believes the other has drowned. Viola dresses in men's clothes, takes the name Cesario, and enters the service of Duke Orsino, who has been hopelessly courting the Countess Olivia. Orsino sends his new page to plead his love to Olivia. Olivia, refusing the Duke, falls in love with the page on sight. Viola, in disguise, has fallen in love with the Duke. The play has its central triangle by the end of Act 1.

In Olivia's household, three resident pranksters — her uncle Sir Toby Belch, his foolish friend Sir Andrew Aguecheek, and her clever waiting-woman Maria — decide to take revenge on Olivia's puritanical steward Malvolio by tricking him into believing his mistress is in love with him. They forge a letter; he reads it; he appears before Olivia smiling, cross-gartered, and in yellow stockings, in obedience to a fantasy. He is locked in a dark room as a madman. Meanwhile, the lost twin Sebastian arrives in town. He looks exactly like Cesario. He meets Olivia, who marries him by mistake. By Act 5 every disguise has unravelled.

Shakespeare wrote Twelfth Night around 1601, the same year as Hamlet. He gave it the alternate title 'What You Will,' meaning: whatever you make of it. It is one of his most often staged comedies and contains some of his richest comic writing — Feste the fool, Sir Toby's drinking scenes, the gulling of Malvolio — alongside its serious centre: Viola's grief, Olivia's mourning, and the question of how exactly someone falls in love with a person in disguise.

angleCards.title: Viola in disguise.
angleCards.text: Viola spends most of the play as 'Cesario,' a young man, in love with the Duke who treats her as his confidant. The play is full of half-confessions she cannot quite finish. Watch what she says and what she has to leave unsaid.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Viola through her disguise — what she can and cannot say to Orsino, what Olivia thinks she sees in her, and how Shakespeare uses the costume to ask what love actually responds to.

angleCards.title: Malvolio.
angleCards.text: The play's funniest scenes are also its cruellest. Malvolio is a self-important puritan who is gulled into making a fool of himself in yellow stockings and is finally locked in a dark room as a madman. Twelfth Night is the comedy that ends with one character refusing to forgive.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Malvolio plot — the forged letter, the yellow stockings, the dark-room scene, the closing 'I'll be revenged' — and decide what Shakespeare thinks of the joke he set up.

angleCards.title: Music and melancholy.
angleCards.text: Twelfth Night opens with 'If music be the food of love' and closes with Feste alone on stage singing 'The rain it raineth every day.' Between them is a play steeped in song, in twilight, and in a sadness comedy is not supposed to have.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to attend to the music of Twelfth Night — Feste's songs, the Duke's longings, the closing dirge — and read the comedy as one of Shakespeare's most melancholy.

angleCards.title: The twin scene.
angleCards.text: Sebastian and Viola finally meet in Act 5 in front of everyone. Shakespeare lets them spend nearly a hundred lines proving who they are to each other. It is one of his strangest, quietest reunions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Act 5 recognition scene as the play's emotional centre — what the twins ask each other to prove, what is left over after the proof, and how Shakespeare frames the relief of survival.

cast.name: Viola
cast.description: A noblewoman shipwrecked on the coast of Illyria, who believes her brother Sebastian has drowned. She enters Duke Orsino's service disguised as a boy named Cesario, falls in love with him, and is sent to woo his beloved Olivia on his behalf. Shakespeare gives her the play's most quoted soliloquy — 'I am not what I am' — and lets her hold the comedy and the grief in the same scene.

cast.name: Duke Orsino
cast.description: The ruler of Illyria, in love with the idea of being in love with Countess Olivia. He opens the play wallowing in music and self-pity and spends most of it sending his new page Cesario to woo Olivia for him. By the time he understands that Cesario is a woman, he has fallen in love with her too.

cast.name: Olivia
cast.description: A wealthy Illyrian noblewoman in deep mourning for a recently dead brother. She has refused all suitors, including Orsino. She falls in love with Cesario on sight, pursues him, and accidentally marries his identical twin instead. She is more practical and more decisive than any other woman in the play.

cast.name: Malvolio
cast.description: Olivia's puritanical, self-important steward, who disapproves of Sir Toby's drinking and Feste's foolery and harbours secret dreams of marrying his mistress. He is tricked by Maria's forged letter into believing Olivia loves him, appears in yellow stockings to court her, and is shut up as a madman. He leaves the play vowing revenge.

cast.name: Sir Toby Belch
cast.description: Olivia's hard-drinking, loud-voiced uncle, who has been living off her hospitality and her cousin Sir Andrew's purse. He invents the Malvolio prank with Maria, baits Sir Andrew into a duel with Cesario, and ends the play married to Maria for her ingenuity.

cast.name: Feste
cast.description: Olivia's professional clown, who moves between her house and the Duke's and is paid by both. He is the play's most musical voice and its closest thing to a moral consciousness. He delivers the closing song that frames the whole comedy as melancholy in costume.

acclaim.quote: This is justly considered as one of the most delightful of Shakespeare's comedies.
Of all Shakespeare's comedies, Twelfth Night is the one with the strongest hold upon our affections.

whyItMatters.title: The Disguise That Asks What Love Sees
whyItMatters.body: Viola enters Orsino's court in men's clothes in Act 1 and stays in them for almost the entire play. She loves the Duke. The Duke does not know she is a woman. She is sent by him to woo another woman — Olivia — who instantly falls in love with her. Three of the principal love stories of the play involve Viola in disguise, and each works for a different reason. Orsino is drawn to 'Cesario' as a confidant before he ever realises this is a woman; the play asks, gently, whether that is love already. Olivia is drawn to Cesario because of what she takes to be a young man's spirit; the play does not entirely take the joke back even when she switches her affection to Sebastian. Twelfth Night is the Shakespeare comedy that most carefully tests what love responds to: a face, a voice, a manner, a person — and the disguise is the experiment. The Duke's last line in the play, before all the wedding plans, is to keep on calling Viola 'Cesario.' He cannot stop. The play does not insist that he must.

whyItMatters.title: The Cruellest Comedy
whyItMatters.body: Twelfth Night contains one of Shakespeare's funniest set pieces and one of his most disturbing. Sir Toby, Maria, Sir Andrew, and Fabian hide in the box-tree while Malvolio walks the garden imagining out loud what it would be like to be Olivia's husband. Maria has forged a letter in his mistress's hand. He finds it. He reads it. He cross-gartered his way to Olivia in yellow stockings. The audience laughs. Then the conspirators lock him up in a dark room and visit him as a fake exorcist, telling him he is mad. Olivia herself does not know what is happening to her steward for most of an act. When Malvolio is finally released, his last line in the play — 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you' — refuses the comic resolution everyone else accepts. Most stagings now play it as a sour, lingering wound under the closing music. Shakespeare wrote the wedding endings and refused to give Malvolio one. That refusal is the part of the play modern audiences usually take home.

whyItMatters.title: Closing With Rain
whyItMatters.body: Twelfth Night ends with the weddings and the embraces and the unmasking, and then everyone leaves the stage except Feste, who steps forward and sings a song about wind and rain. Each verse moves him through a season of his own life — boyhood, manhood, married life, drunkenness, old age — and each ends with the line 'For the rain it raineth every day.' The final stanza closes the play as a play: 'A great while ago the world begun … but that's all one, our play is done, and we'll strive to please you every day.' Shakespeare has just written the merriest comedy of his middle period, and he chose to close it with a half-melancholy song about everything wearing out. It is one of the most haunting comic endings ever written, and it is the reason critics from Hazlitt to Auden have called Twelfth Night a comedy with the inside of a tragedy. The rain is what the laughter has been keeping out for five acts.
